John Malachi (Interviewed by Bryant DuPre) - (5/5/83):
This is the 5th of May, 1983, up at John Malachi's house in Washington, D.C. This is John's interview for the Oral History Project. Take it away, John.

Thanks, Bryant. I guess I can start off by saying that I've really always seen music literally through the eyes of the piano. I guess that probably goes back to the days when I was fascinated by the keyboard on the old pump organ in my grandmother's house down in North Carolina, where I was born.

I was born in Red Springs, North Carolina, September 6, 1919. As a child, I used to wander into the living room, and they would put me up on the stool and just let me bang on the piano keys. At the same time, my mother used to take me to church, and my grandmother and all my aunts and everyone, they all went to church together. And they would all have a hymn book, singing. So in order to keep me quiet, they would give me a book -- because apparently, if I had a book in my hand, I was quiet. But one day, they noticed they handed me a book that didn't have any musical characters on it. There was staff or G-clef or notes or anything. And it didn't seem to quiet me down. I apparently kept screaming and hollering, as my mother says -- I was about three years old then, I guess. So finally, someone had the idea to give me a hymn book, and right away, it seems as if I was quieted down a little bit.
So I guess I've been hooked as a musician, without even

knowing it, from the time I was born, which is something I am very, very grateful for. People usually say that you're born with a gift or something. Well, I think that if I have a gift, or if anyone has a gift, what it really means is that you have a love for something. And of course, my really...

As I said, in the beginning, my really feelings about any kind of music, it always seems to be through the eyes of the piano. I remember one time reading where...I think it was Andres Segovia made a statement that at some period in his life, he married his guitar. So I don't know... I never quite went through the ceremony of marrying the piano. But I think we struck up kind of a love at first sight thing, just as I said before, where I was always fascinated by the keyboard.

Back in Red Springs, North Carolina, as I first remember, we lived in my grandmother's house, which we always called The Big House. Later on, my brothers and my father and his brothers, my uncles, they built a small little house themselves out about a half-a-mile away from my grandmother's house. I guess you would call it a log cabin of some sort, because they split the rails and built it themselves. My parents stayed there until after my sister was born, which was the third child. I had a brother that was next to me, and then my oldest sister, whose name was Marian, was the third. I guess I was about a little over 4 years old then.
Malachi - 3

The family decided to move to Durham, North Carolina, which is where I started elementary school. I guess when you're that age, around 4 or 5, you really begin to really become aware of your surroundings and going to school and whatever. My mother is the kind of person that always had a thirst for education. She didn't have very much herself. I think she went to about the Eighth Grade, which back during those times for a Black person was a pretty high education to have. If I remember, my father went through about the Third or Fourth Grade.

But anyway, my mother always had this thing for music and education of any kind. As a matter of fact, she taught me to... When I went to elementary school I was 6 years old, and by the time I went to elementary school she had taught me to read and write and add and subtract. So when I got to elementary school, I was a little bit ahead of the game. I guess I had the kindergarten training at home, which I don't remember them even having a kindergarten in school then.

But aside from the fact that she taught me these things, she used to sit around in the evenings, and besides reading the Bible to us, she would talk about her family, in which she had eight brothers. In the wintertime, after they had finished farming or picking cotton or whatever it was that they did, and it was that they did, and it was too cold
Malachi - 4

outside, they would sit around the fireplace and they would play these instruments that they had ordered from Sears and Roebuck, and along with the instruments, I understand, came instructions and little pieces that you could play, a do-it-yourself thing... Anyway, she had a knack, I guess an ear would be better, for remembering the sounds that each one of her brothers made. She would say things like, "My uncle Eulis played the trombone, and Uncle Hezekiah that played the cornet..." I don't remember the respective instruments, but she'd talk about the cornet, the bass horn, and whatever the others played.

But she would mention some pieces they would play in regards to... They would be perhaps "The Star Spangled Banner" or "My Country Tis Of Thee" or "Way Down Upon The Swanee River" and things that they would sit around and play, and she would remember each part and sing these parts to us. She would say, "Yonder Uncle Eulis, he would sing..." -- and she would sing his part. I think he played the trombone. And she would sing the lead cornet part, and then she would sing the harmony parts that went along with that. Then she would say things like... On the "Star Spangled Banner," say, she would say, "That part where it says 'the rocket's red glare,' that really goes up very high" -- and she would sing that. She would say, like, when the "balls bursting in air," how the
Malachi - 5
trombone would repeat it with a phrase that went down. And things like that.

So I began to hear music when I went to school. We would sing things in the classroom and assembly, or in church, and I would hear these different parts. And it just became a part of my listening to music, you know.

I remember in Durham, I had an aunt who had...she also had a little organ type instrument. I don't know what it was called, but it had a keyboard. I used to go by, and by this time sit down and... I've forgot this little thing we used to play. It has a lot of different titles. But it was always a thing that you played in F-sharp, and I think what they called...Oh, what was it? I think they used to call it "Coonsshine(?) Baby" or something like that, "oom-bah, oom-bah, oom-bah-bah."

But every time I saw a keyboard, if I was allowed to, I would sit down and try to fool with it while the family was talking in another room, or the other kids were out playing. There just always seemed to be something about it that grabbed me. It was kind of like a toy, I guess. You can't explain these kind of things. As I look back now, I can see that there must have been something very deep down inside, some attraction there. But as to just what makes these things happen, you know, people have all sorts of things -- you're
Malachi - 6
born with this or that. But there's never an answer for these things.

Anyway, my family stayed in Durham for...I guess we were there for, oh, practically five years. As I remember I was in the Fifth Grade, I think I was ten years old, and my father the year before had come to Washington to work, for the obvious reason -- first of all, work down there must have been not so available, and at the same time, there were other things that Blacks were enduring in the South that Blacks always, ever since slavery, have a tendency to try to move further North in hopes for a better life or something.

Nevertheless, the family moved to Washington, D.C. We came here, and we lived in a house out in sort of the suburbs of Washington called Deanwood, which is not very far now, but then it was quite a ways out, and I think only had streetcars out there. It took you about an hour to come from the center of town out there. And we stayed there a while, but my father, his work being in town, and I guess for some other reasons perhaps, he decided that he wanted to move into the city proper, which was much more expensive as far as living and everything was concern. And I guess against my mother's better wishes, he moved us from a house that was I don't remember how many rooms, but was a comfortable living house, into two rooms. You can imagine, by this time there are five
Malachi - 7

children, and we moved into these two rooms -- a man and his wife and five kids living in two rooms. That means you slept and cooked and everything... My mother was very disappointed by it, but during those days... People think male chauvinism is a problem now. They have no idea how it was then. What the old man said went. And so we stayed at this place. He said that it was temporary until we would get into another place.

Nevertheless, we moved around quite a bit, and I started through school at Garrison School here in Washington. They had to put me back in the Fifth Grade again because it was said that kids that came up from the South weren't up to the curriculum that they had here in Washington. So what I had to do, and again my mother was very mad about this, I had to repeat the Fifth Grade over again, which was one of the most boring years in school that I had, because nothing was interesting. I knew everything in the school... I made all Straight-A's and everything that whole year, as I remember. And I think that might have been something that caused me to have some laxity about liking school after that.

Nevertheless, we moved around from one place to another, trying to get a better place. And finally, we wound up in a house on Fourth and O Streets, Northwest. If I remember, it was 1340 Fourth Street, I believe. At this particular time, I
Malachi - 8
guess I was about 11 years old.

But the most significant thing about that was that just before my thirteenth birthday... As I said before, my birthday is September 6, and I think it was in August, about the middle of August... That's just before my thirteenth birthday. My uncle and my father came to the house with a truck. It was a truck that my uncle used on his job. He worked at a used furniture store, and I guess the guy that had the store used to go buy used furniture and sell it to the Blacks in the ghetto there. Anyway, my father came in with my uncle and they began to unload this piano off of this truck. From what I understand, I learned in later years that he paid about five dollars for the piano.

Anyway, they unloaded the piano and brought it into the house and sat it in the living room. My uncle, who used to... We were always glad to see him because he was always giving us anything from pennies to nickels to dimes or whatever, and we were always glad to see Uncle Jim. Uncle Jim said this particular day, after he sat down at the piano, "Okay. The first one of you kids that learns to play something on this piano, I'm going to give 'em five dollars." Wow, that was a whole lot of money, because then it was during the Depression, and my father had a job where he was making $35 every two weeks. So you can imagine what five dollars meant to a kid --
Malachi - 9

or what it meant to a grown-up, much less a kid.
So when he said this, I guess my ears just perked up. I felt like it was no problem to me, because I liked to fool with this thing anyway. So I sat down, and as I said, by this time it was around 7 o'clock, I guess. And by the time I went to bed that night, at 10:30 or 11 o'clock, I was playing a piece with two fingers, two-part harmony... But I had learned this little piece that we used to sing in Sunday School and at school, too, a piece called "Lift Every Voice and Sing," but which later became what was called "The National Negro Anthem" -- it still is. It's a very beautiful piece. I learned the first strain of it, but the bridge gets a little complicated. But I felt like that was enough to get me over with my uncle, and the next day, or whenever he did come back, I would have it all for him -- or I was hoping.

I didn't see my uncle for another three or four weeks. And the fact is that I never did get the five dollars. But if there's anyone I am grateful to, it's my Uncle Jim for, I guess, spurring me on like that to play. I don't think that he would have had to do that, but it did help a little bit. And of course, I have a lot of other people to thank for it.
But from that day on, it was every day at the piano. School started about two-three weeks from there. And I remember when I went to school I could hardly wait to get back
Malachi - 10

home to sit down and play my piano. The first thing I'd do, I'd come in, and if I had some chores to do, I would get it over fast, homework or whatever, and I'd spend the rest of the evening, until I went to bed, banging this piano. Every day I'd gain a little more, I'd learn a little something else. I finally found out how I could put three of the keys together and get a different sound. There would always be a sound that I... It was like finding something that you were looking for and knew it was there or something, because I knew the sound back to these different harmonies that my mother was singing.

At the same time, we had this old gramophone in the house, which you manually wound it with a crank, and it had this dog sitting on it listening... It had a horn, and it was always called... I think it was a RCA Victor slogan or something, and it said 'His Master's Voice' on there. Anyway, older people would remember that. If not, you can always go down to the museum and find these things. But we had a few records. And two records that I remember were... Or not two records, but two people that I remember were Bessie Smith and Louis Armstrong. Three maybe, and that was Mamie Smith. Which I always thought Bessie and Mamie Smith were sisters; I learned later that they weren't.
We had a record of Louis Armstrong singing... One was 'When It's Sleepy Time Down South,' the other was 'I Got A
Malachi - 11

Right To Sing The Blues"... We had about four Louis Armstrong ones. And we had Bessie Smith, I forgot which of the blues that she would sing, but all of them were what I thought then was typical blues, which I learned later, they were always a little bit different in the harmonic structure. But most of them were basic blues things. And of course, the same thing happened with Mamie Smith.

Another record I remember us having, which I didn't comprehend too much right then was a thing called "Ring Dem Bells" by Duke Ellington. That was a little bit heavy for me then. The only thing I remember about that was this guy would hit what I later learned were chimes, and the band would answer with... I think there was a vocalist on that, too -- on "Ring Dem Bells."

But this was the kind of musical atmosphere that I was in, and it kind of helped me... I used to try to pick these things out on the piano. "Sleepy Time Down South" was a major accomplishment, because it started off with a chord, and then I think it was... Now that I know it, one was a major chord, and then you moved one tone and it became a minor, and it just made a beautiful sound to me. I really felt like I was growing in a harmonic sense.
In the meantime, I was in junior high school. The first junior high school I went to was Shore Junior High School,

which was then at Rhode Island Avenue and Seventh Street. It was a very nice junior high school. I heard a young pianist there who... I don't know if he was in the same grade I was, or maybe he might have been a grade ahead of me -- because, as I said, I was put back a grade when I came in. Anyway, the grade doesn't matter. But he was a young fellow, actually a couple of years younger than I am. But he used to play the piano around the school and all the kids knew him and everything. And I listened to him, and he would play things by Fats Waller, like "I'm Gonna Sit Right Down and Write Myself a Letter." He would do things with both hands, you know, and had a little what we know now as stride and all that he would play.

And I just thought it was fantastic that he could do this, but at the same time, I would try to duplicate these things myself. We didn't have any records by Fats Waller at that particular time, but every now and then you would hear a record somewhere. We didn't have a radio either. But I would hear a record of this pianist, Fats Waller, and I would try to pick out things like that.

After being there a year, I was transferred to another junior high school. It seems as if the area that I was living in was re-zoned or something, and I went to this other school called Terrell Junior High School. And at Terrell, I met this
Malachi - 13

kid that played guitar, played the four-string guitar. He found out that I could dabble on the piano, because what would happen was that sometimes I would slip into the assembly when nobody was in there, and start pecking around with the piano until some teacher chased me off it.

And a couple of times he heard me, and he and I became friends. He says, "I play the guitar." So I asked him to come by my house. He came by the house, and we sat down, and he would play little things and I would try to find it on the piano. And finally, we had a little repertoire of about four or five pieces, and some other little things that were called shouts, which was actually three or four chords doing some sort of rhythmical thing.

But anyway, he was telling me about these parties that he played sometimes where he could make some money. He said he'd make sometimes 75 cents or a dollar with another guitar. Or I don't know if he'd been playing with any pianists or not... But he asked me if I would like to try that, and I just went "Yeah!" The idea of playing for anybody was fine with me. I didn't have no idea about how much I didn't know. The fact that I could sit down and play one piece for anybody, I thought it was a major accomplishment.
Anyway, these were what were then called house hops, which were actually house rent parties, where people were...
Malachi - 14

As I said before, it was during the Depression and money was very scarce, and people in the ghetto gave these parties and things, and whoever was working came. And they would sell food, what is known now as Soul Food -- it's a later term. But they'd sell things like chitlins and collard greens, pig's feet and potato salad. And we always had the neighborhood chemist that would come around and mix up a beverage, mixed it in a bathtub someplace, and mixed with alcohol, and they'd come up with a vintage 1931 White Lightnin' it was called then -- I guess for most people it was the relative to corn whiskey. But that was the fare that they would have at these particular things.

So Herman... I don't remember exactly the first one that we got, but I started doing these things with him. Sometimes we'd make 50 cents between us, and sometimes we would make 50 cents each -- which in junior high school for us was, you know, a penny earned, a penny gained I guess! The main thing, we were having fun doing it, and we had these grown-ups that were more or less encouraging us by hiring us, and as we played these things, they would dance.

So in this atmosphere, I began to... Whenever I would play one of these things, invariably there would be some more mature pianist or an adult pianist that would come in and sit down and play. Someone would say, "Oh, here comes so-and-so-
Malachi - 15
and-so,"or "here comes this one or that one," and they had pianists that I remember...

One in particular was a big guy that always impressed me as being a typical laborer-looking type fellow, big arms, strong. Everybody called him Kid Norfolk. And Kid Norfolk, I think, could play in maybe one or two keys, F or F-sharp or C-sharp. And he would sit down and he would really make that piano ring. Most of the pianos were old upright pianos then, and he had this very strong left hand, and being physically strong himself, you could hear him all through the neighborhood. And people would come, and even stand outside the house and stand out in the streets to listen to Kid Norfolk play. I was just mesmerized by hearing someone play like that, because I had never heard anyone really play the piano. The only time I'd heard the piano played was either in church or in Sunday School or in the school.

Then there were other pianists. There was another fellow, Kid Socks(?), who played very good piano in that particular what they called House Hop style. Then there were a couple of other pianists that occasionally would come into these places who had a little better status. They were with a group... I remember a group called the Four Dots that was very popular around here, and they used to broadcast on the radio once a week. They had a pianist, his name was Toya(?). I
Malachi - 16
don't know whether that was his first name or last name -- Toya(?).

Then there was another guy, a very tall guy. I guess he was about the first I guess seven-foot person that I ever saw. They called him Piano Slim. He played very good. He later went with a group called The Three Keys, which were more or less of national fame. He replaced their pianist, I think... Which I think they were located in Philadelphia.

But then, hearing all these pianists, I couldn't wait to get home the next day to play what I thought I heard and try to duplicate some of what was happening. I would always come up with something that made it all worthwhile.

Meantime, I had a couple of aunts that lived with us, my father's sisters, and they were in high school. They were just beginning to go to dances, and they had boyfriends. This one guy was going with my younger Aunt Pearl that used to come around to see her. And like, young boys always seem to have a thing that when they go see the girl at that age, they always carry a guy with them -- for what reason I never did quite understand! But I guess I used to do the same thing myself.

But anyway, this fellow used to come to see my Aunt. And he'd have this other guy with him, which I later learned his name was James Morgan, and he could play the piano. He was just, I guess I feel like, the first real pianist that I think
Malachi - 17

I ever heard. James Morgan was sort of known as a child prodigy. At that time, I was I guess about 14 years old, and James Morgan was about 18 then. Anyway, he would come to our house and he would play, and I just couldn't believe a piano could sound that beautiful. He'd play some of the popular things, like... I remember, he was the first one that I think I heard play "Sophisticated Lady," and there was a tune out there, popular then, called "Out In The Cold Again." The one that I was really impressed with was a thing called "Blue Moon." It seemed in the part of it which I know now as the bridge, it changed keys and went through something...it seemed like it went to another key or modulation or something -- it was just thrilling to me.

But this fellow used to play all of these things. His name was James Morgan. He just died. I think James Morgan died around 1978. He was the kind of guy that never left Washington -- for what reasons, I don't know, because everybody would try to get him to leave. Other bandleaders would come here, and try to coax him away from Washington. But as far as I know, James Morgan never went across the bridge to Alexandria, Virginia.
Nevertheless, he was very good, and at that particular age he had a broadcast, Monday through Friday, at 12 noon on station WRC. They called the program James Morgan At The
Malachi - 18

Piano. I think it was about a half-an-hour. I would have my ears glued to somebody's radio listening to James Morgan. And this really began to... There's an expression used, "My nose was pretty wide-open for the piano."

Although I never thought of it as a livelihood or whatever, I can remember at the same time where my relatives, my uncles or aunts, would come around and they would always ask (there's five kids in the family and all of this) "What do you want to be when you grow up?" And my brother always had a ready answer. He'd say "a carpenter" or whatever came into his mind, and they were always admiring him, you know. They'd ask me, and I would say, "I don't know." And at the same time, I never had the connection of me playing the piano and making any money. That wasn't the idea at all! I just liked to play the piano like it was a toy or something.

But as I began to hear these different pianists, I just wanted to hear more and more. At the same time, it was around the time when I heard my first big band. That was just around the same time I think I took my first date, the first date I ever took a girl on -- I was 14. I took her up to the Howard Theatre. I didn't know who was there. All I knew was that my aunts used to tell me they had shows up there and everything, and they had they had these bands. So I thought I'm going to be a big shot, and I'd made 50 cents or 75 cents, so I was
Malachi - 19

going to show this girl that I really knew what was happening. She didn't know that I had never been inside the theatre myself. But I took her to the Howard Theatre, and we sat in the balcony. All of a sudden, after the picture... When we went in, the picture was on. Then after the picture, the lights came on.

There's a fellow, Shep Allen, that just passed away recently, who was a legend with the Howard Theatre here in Washington, or was a legend with the theatre. He made this announcement that "Next week's coming revue..." The next band the following week was going to be Chick Webb, and... He used to use the expression "Chick Webb's band with a gala revue." He would say, "And now, ladies and gentlemen, for your listening pleasure, Fletcher Henderson." And the band would start to play behind the curtain, and the curtain would slowly open up, and you'd see these brilliant lights, and these guys sitting on the stage with this all... All the bands always had fine uniforms then. And there would be Fletcher Henderson standing in front of the band with a baton. They'd play the first number, and he would announce the second one. Sometimes he would start the band off, and then sit down at the piano, and other times he would just conduct the band through the whole number. But most times, he would start the band off and sit down.
Malachi - 20

But all of this was very fascinating to me. And I was kind of torn between watching this lady, or trying to approach this young lady on my first date and what was going on up there on the stage, and listening to the band, and trying to listen to what the piano player was playing.

Anyway, I liked that. So the next week, I found myself up there to hear Chick Webb. I heard Chick Webb's band, and I never will forget... I thought that the guy who was standing in front of the band was Chick Webb. And for a long time, it was quite a while, that somebody told me that the guy in front of the band wasn't Chick Webb; his name was Bardu Ali. At that particular time, all the bands had some character standing up there waving a stick in front of the band, and a lot of times it was not the bandleader who was doing it. In Chick Webb's case, he was the drummer in the and, and I also learned later that he had this physical disability that it wasn't convenient for him to come out on the stage. So Bardu Ali did all the MC'ing and the waving his hands in front of the band as the conductor.

I enjoyed listening to it. But there was so much going on, you didn't know where to really center your attention. At that particular time, I guess I was so I guess enchanted with everything that was going on on the stage, that I didn't settle in on any one instrumentalist. I always did try to
Malachi - 21

hear what the piano player was doing. But somehow, I couldn't hear the piano player, because I didn't know how to listen to him. He was playing the chords in the band, but the horns and everything were... My ears weren't that sensitive to actually center the piano player out. But I would watch him anyway. There were guys that had all sorts of ways of sitting sideways at the piano, and all sorts... Which was very interesting to me, you know.

I guess the first band that really made me decide that I wanted to play the piano all my life was when I heard Duke Ellington's band. And in Duke's band I could hear the piano, because Duke played the piano... No matter what was happening, he played with a very dominating force, and you could hear him... He had a little way that he played his accompaniment that was very unique. Besides the way he...
[END OF TAPE 1, SIDE 1]

Besides the way Duke looked, because he was always a sharp dresser, which was very attractive to young men in those days, and he was a very good-looking guy, and his mannerisms and everything just made me set all eyes on Duke Ellington.
But I guess the thing that really brought the thing to a climax when I heard him, was when he sat down and played this
Malachi - 22

same "Sophisticated Lady" himself on the piano, and the way he played it just seemed to make an impression. I always feel like that particular moment was what made me realize that I wanted to play the piano more than anything in my life. I still didn't think of myself playing it as a profession or a livelihood. Before it had been something that I did, and I did it between baseball and football, and playing out with other kids -- it was just something that I could do. But when I heard this, I just felt like there was really something happening with playing the piano.

So, if I can digress a little bit, oh, about six or seven months after my uncle and my father brought this piano to the house, I had been coming in every evening, sitting and playing, and no one ever had to tell me to practice or anything like that. So they just let me play as much as I wanted to. And my mother was always very encouraging. And my father decided he would give me piano lessons. Well, there was a fellow, one of the friends of my father that used to come around, and he would play for little get-togethers that he would have at the house with the people from the various committees, the church or whatever, and he would have this friend... This fellow's name was Jack Smith. I never did know what happened to Jack Smith, but he was always what I thought of as a very good pianist. Anyway, I used to love to listen
Malachi - 23
to him, too. But my father decided that he would have Jack give me some piano lessons.

So when he told me about it, he said, "Mr. Smith is going to come by and give you some piano lessons, and he says he'll be by on Tuesday" or something. I could hardly wait, because this guy...to come and push this magic button and make me a pianist. But when he came in, I was sitting at the piano, I had been sitting at the piano for the last hour... He came in and he listened to a few little things I did, and then he sat down and played a couple of pieces. I was admiring him, and he said, "Oh, you liked that?" I said, "Yeah." So he said, "Okay, come on and sit down." And I sat down at the piano, and he learned over my shoulder and said, "Put your hand here and put your hand here, and put this finger here..."

As he was doing this, he was showing me these things on the keyboard, my father came in -- I guess a half-hour or an hour later, while he was doing it. And my father stopped him and asked to speak to him for a minute. And my father took him sort of over in the corner, and I heard them talking, and kind of in low tones. What I heard my father say was... He told this fellow Jack, "I don't ever want you ever to come back here like that again, and I don't want him taught like that." He was referring to me.
So the next thing I knew, Jack had his coat and hat and
Malachi - 24

was leaving. I was a little puzzled, but I don't... I didn't ask them for what reasons... I don't know why I didn't ask. At that particular time he had Pearl Bailey singing up there, and a couple of other girls. That was my job. I played the piano for them, and sang, and played a few little things that I knew myself. And then, when showtime came, it would feature Jelly Roll Morton, and he would sit down and play and talk to the people about New Orleans and all of that. I always wondered then why, being on U Street and everything,
Malachi - 48

the audience he had always was White, and they would come up and they would be in big limousines and Cadillacs, and they all looked like wealthy people. But Blacks very seldom went in there to hear him at all! Which I learned later what it was really all about.

But he would give this show, and he would talk about the old days in New Orleans, and played different tunes and demonstrations of what was going on. One of his very popular things, besides a thing he used to play called "Milenberg Joys" and "Muskrat Ramble," a thing he used to play called "The Pearls"... But the most popular thing was... He climaxed it when he'd play "Tiger Rag" and he'd make the tiger roar throwing his forearm on the bass of the keyboard, up on the bass side, and they go WRRROOMPPP, and "Hold that tiger, WRRROOMPPP." That just made the people go into ecstasy, you know...!

But later on... There was a guitarist that a friend of mine around here that played with Bill Baldwin's band. I happened to be up on U Street one afternoon and asked him where he was going. He said, "I'm going with Jelly Roll down to the Library of Congress." He said, "We've been going down and recording every day down there." I learned later that Jelly Roll made some very historical recordings down there that, from what I understand, are still there. But I had no
Malachi - 49

idea just who I was talking to, and I have to say that quite a few years later, I began to read and really know about who Jelly Roll was. Because then he was just a braggart old man that played old-time piano, you know. I even at one time thought that maybe he might have been Bessie Smith's boyfriend or something because she used to sing about jelly rolls! I had no idea that it was a real live man named Jelly Roll.

In the meantime, while I was playing up at this place, in the daytime I was always at my house playing. And this kid, Oswald Gibson, the saxophone player, had gone back in school... By this time I was out of school... Because I had met this fellow, Robert Harley, that I had known from the neighborhood in the earlier days, when he and I played piano... He had a sister, and her name was Rhoda. I had known her since I was... Well, actually I met him when I was about 13, and I had known her since she was about 12. And you know, like all young kids I didn't like her because she always seemed to be in the way, and I didn't particularly like her at all. Like, I didn't even care that much about girls then anyway, like most boys... Anyway, as fate would have it, a couple of years later she began to look different to me, which really wound up with him being my brother-in-law! Of course, she was my wife. And right after my seventeenth birthday was when I got married, and I fell out of high school.

But this kid, Oswald Gibson, was still there in high school. He was at Armstrong High School, the same high school that I had gone to. As a matter of fact, he was in high school with my brother, who was younger than I. And they had a band down there, and these kids in the band... A fellow named professor had the band. And these kids in the band, a couple of them were trying to learn and had been listening to Jazz and musicians and whatever. This fellow Oswald Gibson... There was another saxophone player, Wash we used to call him... What was his first name...? And he had a brother, James Washington, who played trumpet. Finally, he later got the name Stumpy Red that everybody called him, because he was short... Anyway, he and his brother were both in Armstrong, along with my brother, who had by this time started playing trumpet. All of them... By me playing around in clubs and everything, I was considered a rather senior musician to them, as though I was a couple of years older and everything... So we used to get together at the house and play.

One of the fellows that used to come by the same club where I used to meet all of these musicians was a fellow whose name was Billy Roberts. He played the guitar. Billy Roberts was a grown man, and... Somehow he got the idea in his head that he would like to have a band of youngsters. By knowing me... I don't know whether he had heard of Oswald Gibson or
Malachi - 51
not. But anyway, he came by my house one day and told me, told us rather, that he'd like to form this band if we could get some more guys. Of course, we told him, sure, we could.

There was a guy that lived in Oswald Gibson's neighborhood. As a matter of fact, they kind of grew up together, I guess. His name was George Brown. Later they gave him the name of Dude Brown, for certain reasons which maybe I'll get a chance to talk about later. But Dude Brown, George Brown was a drummer. A fellow, William Eldridge, who is a cousin to Roy Eldridge, was also at Armstrong High School, played bass. And we had a trumpet player, our first trumpet player, that later went to Philadelphia and later played with Louis Jordan and a lot of bands -- his name was Bert Payne. I think Bert is still in Philadelphia. He played trumpet... Well, he could actually play the guitar, too, but he played trumpet with our band. There was another trumpet player whose name was Oliver... Altogether we wound up with... Oh, Edward Griffin was the tenor saxophone; we called him Bubbus -- Bubbus Griffin. The other saxophone player was Frank Wess.

Now, Oswald Gibson, Frank Wess and Nathan Washington (because Nathan was his name) all played alto saxophones. Bubbus was the only one that played tenor. So, this fellow Billy Roberts said, "Look, we can't have three alto saxophones
Malachi - 52

and one tenor." He said, "One of you'all should play tenor." So he looked at Frank Wess and told Frank Wess, "With your tone, I think you should be a tenor player." We were young, we didn't know what he was talking about. Later, I felt like I disagreed with his decision a lot, because Frank Wess played very good alto, and clarinet and everything -- he was always a good reader.

Anyway, Frank Wess went home. The next day he came back, and he had a tenor saxophone. So that completed our reed section. And there was a fellow named Orville Pace who played trombone. So we had three trumpets, one trombone, four saxophones, and we had four in the rhythm section. I can't remember who the guitar player was.

But anyway, this fellow, he had the band and he rehearsed it two or three times, but he never got a job or anything for us. He just sort of (?) rehearsing. Finally I think he kind of lost interest, or maybe some attempts he had made to try to sell it running up against competition with the other more mature bands -- as I said, they had five of them. So with him trying to get a bunch of kids to play somewhere, I guess it probably didn't seem very profitable.
So when he dropped the band, we continued it, and that was when I began my I guess second and real serious stage and trying to arrange. So what we would do, we would buy stock
Malachi - 53

arrangements. There was a fellow who was an excellent musician, played with Duke Ellington, or wrote music for Duke and everything, and later sort of came to kind of a tragic end... Because as a young man he was very brilliant; I think he graduated from Juilliard. His name was Billy White. He played with Duke briefly in the Forties, and he was the kind of a guy that could have... He was ahead of his time, really, because he could have been an excellent contract musician As a clarinet player, anyone who ever heard him play Classical or... Well, he wasn't too much of a Jazz player, but his Classical...and technique and everything... He also studied with this famous clarinet player with the Marine band. I don't remember what his name was, but he was quite a renowned clarinet player at that particular time.

So this fellow's name was Billy White, and he used to write us some arrangements. And then listening to records, we would pick out things that the bands were playing and try to duplicate them. In the meanwhile, I would get some brilliant idea and I would sit down at the piano, and I would make a chord for somebody and tell each saxophone what to play, then I would make another one and tell the trumpets what to play, and tell the other guys, and then just hit it and see what it sounds like. Then that sounds good, so then I'd give them another chord.
Malachi - 54

After that, one time I got the idea to write some whole notes behind... This record, "Muskrat Ramble"... I don't remember, it might have been Benny Goodman's group. It was a small group... No, Lionel Hampton. Lionel Hampton and I think Benny Goodman might have been on the record. But it featured a tenor solo by Hershel Evans, a beautiful solo. And the tenor player learned this solo from listening to the record. So what I did, I found out what the chords were, and I gave the band the chords to play behind him on the solo, you know. And we played it, and everybody dug it!

So then I began to write out backgrounds for maybe the saxophones and have a trumpet player play a lead or something like that. It got so that where all the kids were starting their chords and everything, and we'd get... We had a system where in a chord, I would say somebody played a root, somebody else played a third and somebody else played a fifth, and I'd stand in front of the band and have somebody play the lead, and call the chords out to the brass section, and they'd take their respective notes and they'd just play. So in doing that, I later began to be able to write a few little things myself. In the meantime, I was learning a little bit about syncopation and all that. One thing led to another, and the next thing I knew, I was writing these little arrangements, which is a great thing.
Malachi - 55

And that little band went on for I guess two or three years, with different changes in it. The last one we had, Osie Johnson was the drummer in it. Because somewhere in there came the War, and Frank Wess went in the Army... As a matter of fact, this fellow, Sergeant Price from Howard University, came on, and he broke the band up, really -- because he took Frank Wess, he took Oswald Gibson, he took my brother, and I think Bubbus went with him. Anyway, the band was shattered. And what few guys were left, we billed it... We got it back together again with Osie Johnson and some other guys.

But all the while this was going on, I was playing jobs at night with older musicians. For a long time when I worked around Washington, I was the youngest musician in the band. After the stint that I had with Jelly Roll Morton up there at the Jungle Inn, I think I made... I got a little band of my own, I believe, for a short while, and then came this thing where the WPA, which was...
Works Progress Administration.

...a thing that Franklin D. Roosevelt had implemented -- Work Projects Administration, I think it was called, or something like that. Anyway, it was known as the WPA. What it meant was that it actually gave people jobs that ranged from guys working in labor work, professionals, artists and
Malachi - 56

what have you. Tommy Miles' band had... What they did actually... Like, in mostly governmental things that don't run quite true to what they're supposed to be. The guys who headed the Arts things in the WPA came up and recruited Tommy Miles' whole band, because he wanted to make his project look good, you know. And doing that, there again, somebody sought me out to join this thing and play with the band.

Meanwhile, I had this young family and everything. They said there was regular money and it meant that we played a minimum of twice a week... We played places like the hospitals, we played St. Louis Elizabeth Hospital every Tuesday. We played schools and all sorts of government places. And what we did every day was rehearse. So this is where I really had a chance to stretch out my arranging and everything. Before that, I had written this little thing that my band had been playing. I don't know what we called it, but it had a strong influence of Jimmy Lunceford's band. When I joined this band, which was a bigger and better band, the guys could really play, I just called it... What did I call it...? They had a thing, a slip of paper, that whatever...you were going to get sacked on the program... They called this paper a 403, and if you got a 403 that means that was your walking papers for one reason or another. So I labeled this thing "Opus 403," which later became "Opus X." But I guess I wrote
Malachi - 57
it when I was about 19 years old.

I wrote a lot of music with that band, and I played with some excellent musicians. I played a lot of different kind of music, and I think that's where I got my real professional training as a musician.

Also, we rehearsed every day, and once a week we had a harmony teacher that came in, and we studied theoretical harmony. It was all a government thing. So all of that, with me working in music 24 hours a day, helped me to do a lot of what I wanted to do. We had two hours rehearsal, and the job in the evening was two hours. And most times, the evenings that we worked, we didn't rehearse.

We had some funny incidents happen that show you the vanity of young people, young men especially. At that particular time I felt like I was really doing it. I was beginning to meet some of these people I had seen at the Howard Theatre, began to meet them personally. I really felt like I was really a musician.

I think I was about 20 years old, and we played the Bureau of Engraving -- we played a dance down there for some reason or another; it was a government thing. It was in the evening. When we started playing, I had on this brand-new black suit. We used to wear what we called a tuxedo effect, which means that you wore a black suit or a blue suit with a
Malachi - 58

white shirt, and you got a maroon bow tie and a maroon boutonniere. So on the stage it looked like you might have had a tuxedo on. So what we call a tuxedo effect, that was our uniform. So it meant that we could economize by wearing it wherever else we went, at church, or a social function you went to, or anything. In other words, you could wear it as a street suit, and you didn't have to buy a tuxedo.

So I had this brand-new, tailor-made black suit on that night. I really thought I was sharp. And I'm playing. In the meantime, there's a guy going around with a camera, taking pictures. So when I saw him, I approached him and asked him what was he doing. He said he was taking pictures. I said, 'For what particular purpose?' He said, 'For any purpose.' I said, 'Well, I'd like to get a picture of me. How much?' So he told me what it would cost and everything And I think I had him make me three or four of them; it wasn't that expensive. I said, 'You can just let me know when you're ready.'

So something was going on, and the band wasn't playing at that particular time, and we were still sitting on the stage. And while I was sitting there... Eleanor Roosevelt, Mrs. Franklin Delano Roosevelt was there, and she was to make a speech later. But in the meaning, while this other person was talking or... I don't know what was happening. But we were
Malachi - 59
just sitting there, and she stood behind me with both hands on my shoulders, you know..>
Who did?

Eleanor Roosevelt. So while she's doing this, at some time or another, the photographer winked at me and told me "Let's do it now" -- which meant that he was going to take my picture. I politely turned around to Mrs. Roosevelt and asked her did she mind moving; this gentleman was going to take my picture. And now I still have that picture, and it's a picture that reminds me til the day I die that if I ever thought I was smart, that was one time when I look at that picture, I know what a fool I was! Because I can see her standing behind me in that picture, and it would have been something I would have treasured for life. But my young vanity told me... What did I care about Eleanor Roosevelt? I was concerned about me and blue suit and my piano in this picture. It's just one of those things that you do when you're young, because you have no idea what a fool you are. But that picture stands as a reminder all the time, to me. If I ever want to think I'm smart, I go look at that and say, "Well, if you think you're smart, that's one time you can take a good look at a fool."
But all in all, you know, the experience with the Tommy Miles band was just an experience that I think really brought
Malachi - 60

me into the professional thing. That was finally when I really decided that I'm not going to do anything else; you're doing this and... I would go from one job to another, and I never had another job doing anything else since I was a kid. I sold newspapers, but since I'd started playing the piano I've never had another job doing anything else. So during this time, when I began to write and everything, I said... I don't know, a lightbulb or something came up in my head, saying, "Look, you're a professional musician. What else are you waiting for?"

In the meantime, in 1938, I was made to join the union for some job that I was on -- I don't remember which one. But even after I joined the union, I hadn't considered myself a professional musician. But when after I'd worked with Tommy Miles' band and began to meet all these professionals, guys that would come to the theatre and all of that, then I decided I'd just as soon do this as anything else, and what else did I want to do -- I couldn't think of anything else.

In the meantime, there were a couple of clubs down at Seventh and T Streets, Northwest, where... I would go in there after I got off work... There was a known after-hours place called the Footlight Club, which was run by a fellow called Freddie Woods. And that was where all the musicians and anybody who came in town used to congregate. Because during
Malachi - 61

those days you had the segregated things going on. Everytown USA had a Harlem USA, which meant that there was a place where Blacks lived and congregated and everything. So U Street and Seventh and T were the highlight of this particular area, and Seventh and T being around the corner from the Howard Theatre... This Footlight Club, when people played the Howard Theatre, they all came there. They had food and drink and, you know, they just congregated... I don't ever remember them having any other music up there but a piano.

This is where I met this fellow Toby Walker, who I was saying was my first real contact with a person I thought was a genius. And I actually became acquainted with him, and would go up there every night religiously to listen to him and have him dazzle me with what he was doing. And he liked me very much.

When I'd go up there at night... I would walk in there one night, there would be Duke Ellington, there would be Johnny Hodges or Sonny Greer, people out of Duke's band. Another night it would be guys... At that particular time Ben Webster was with Cab Calloway. There would be people like Ben Webster... Them guys were celebrities. I didn't know who they were a lot of times, but the older musicians said, "That's so-and-so-and-so, and he's this and he's that."
Some of the guys that I worked with around here, who we
Malachi - 62

really became fast friends... There was one guy, Leonard Phillips -- we called him Phil. He was a trumpet player. And he and another fellow, Otto Jones... I think Otto's from Arkansas. As a matter of fact, I think they're both from Arkansas, Phil and Otto. [BOTH ARE FROM WARREN, ARKANSAS] They were older guys, and they knew all these people. They would say, "That's Ben Webster" and "That's Chu Berry" and "That's Roy Eldridge."

There was this guitar player that worked with Booker Coleman and taught me a lot about chords; his name was Sammy Woods. Just to show you how things change, and different... Roy Eldridge used to come to Washington here. When he was in town, Sammy would have his guitar, and he'd have a string around his neck, and he would go around and see Roy. Between shows, Roy would come out with his horn and a mute. And they would walk, like... The Howard Theatre was at Wilberg(?) and T Street, which is between Sixth and Seventh. Well, when you walk around Sixth Street, it's just residential. And Sammy and Roy... Roy would get his horn and his mute, and Sammy with his guitar, and they would walk around there through the streets and smoke a joint, and they'd play, he strumming the guitar and Roy playing... They'd walk through the street, and nobody paid any attention to anybody. Smoking pot was just something nobody paid any attention to. They'd do it right on
Malachi - 63

the streets of downtown Washington, if you wanted to. I guess if people had knowledgeable, they might have said something. There were a lot of times things said about "people who smoke reefers are crazy" and all that, but that's about as far as it went. People sang songs about it...
"Chant of the Weed."
Yes. You know, "Reefer Man." Cab Calloway sang "Reefer Man." He had a thing about "a reefer five feet long."
Anyway, things like that were happening. And these guys that I knew, like Sammy Woods and Leonard Phillips...
