There was another tenor saxophone player, Paul Jones. There was Buster McPherson, an alto player -- he was a very good alto player. Paul Jones was the leading tenor player in town, and he used to battle with all the tenor saxophonists that came in town -- guys like, you know, Chu Berry and Ben Webster and all of them would come in there. In those days guys would come in looking for Paul Jones, or he'd be looking for them, or one of those kind of things. They'd have really these friendly battles. And they'd really play, you know!
Roy Eldridge...one of the more famous types of things that happened like that was with him. And a guy who had him

in Washington, who I understand had kind of come up with Rex Stewart... His name was Danny Bashears(?), and everybody called him "Georgetown." Georgetown, like James Morgan who I mentioned earlier, was a trumpet player that never left Washington, D.C. But he played as good as anybody in the country, including... I understand... I didn't hear the battle that they had, but I understand that Roy Eldridge came in town, and he and Georgetown had it, and it was 50-50 as to who was playing what. I later heard Georgetown, as a matter of fact I worked with him in later years. I was around, but I wasn't at that particular incident when it happened. But I worked with him later. And as a trumpet player, any trumpet player today would admire him, because he had all the qualities of playing... He had the technique and he had the feeling, he knew what he was doing -- the whole thing. The other thing about him, he had no desires to travel. He had many offers from Duke Ellington and Basie, Earl Hines, all of them, to travel, but he elected to just stay here. There are some guys that are like that, who aren't seeking the fame and fortune, the road... They're not seeking it or they're afraid of what might happen when they go out or something.
But all that was quite a learning experience to me in hearing these people play.
Going back a little bit, around 1936, all of a sudden
Malachi - 65

this new band jumped into popularity. Everybody was listening to Jimmy Lunceford and Duke Ellington and Fletcher Henderson, Chick Webb, Earl Hines -- these were the major bands. All of a sudden, this band came with this number that was called "One O'Clock Jump." And it was a band called Count Basie. So everybody said, "Here comes another band. There's Duke Ellington, Cab Calloway -- here comes some guy who's a count." But then when you began to listen to the band, it had something different about it in every kind of way. There were no bands that were sounding like that. And all of the bands that came through here... They had bands like McKinney's Cotton Pickers... Every major band that you can think of came through here. But Basie had this different kind of a sound.

I'll never forget the time that they first came to the Howard Theatre. The bus used to stop right there on T Street and unload the musicians, and they'd go find their respective hotels or rooms or whatever. Most of the guys would wind up going in this place, you know. So it happens that the tenor saxophone player with the Basie band, Lester Young, had been long, lifetime friends with Leonard Phillips. I don't know whether Otto Jones was in that particular thing or not... Yeah, yes he was. So anyway, I got to meet Lester Young through them.
And of course, there was another hook-up that I
Malachi - 66

understand happened when I just happened not to be on the scene -- Lester Young's thing with Paul Jones. I got stories about it... Always stories like that are conflicting, you know. Naturally, Phil and Otto, being from out West and everything, and having a different feeling about things... Phil could give you the impression that Lester had walked in and walked all over top of Paul, you know. Well, I wasn't there, so I can't say. But I know that Paul was an excellent saxophone player, and there's no question about Lester Young. Nevertheless, this is just one of those incidents that happened.

But I got to know Lester, and from then on, after that, when Lester came in town, soon as he got off the bus he was right in this club. There were times when, after this fellow, Toby Walker, had finished playing up there and everybody would go home -- that's usually around 5 o'clock in the morning -- Lester and I would still be sitting in there until sun-up, sometimes 10 o'clock in the morning, just he and playing. Which I was happy to do, because at that particular time he was recording with Billie Holiday and Teddy Wilson and he was making a lot of those things that since then have become collector's things, I guess, or... Well, they are collectors items... But they are historic recordings, you know -- the Teddy Wilson-Billie Holiday-Lester Young things that they
Malachi - 67

recorded. And a lot of those tunes, Lester when he came down here would have just come from New York, and they'd just tunes. He would sit there, and he would ask if I knew this or this, and I'd say "No" -- he would teach it to me right there.

All of this was in this learning process of me meeting some of the greatest musicians in the world, and a lot of times not even being aware of just really how great they were! But all these people used to come...if they came to Washington, they came up to Freddy Woods' place.

Toby Walker, if I can go back to him, was a fabulous pianist. They had a thing, it was sort of a phenomenon I guess you'd call it, that people would come far and wide and give him five dollars to play George Gershwin's "I Got Rhythm" very fast, and play it for an hour himself. And many times I walked in the club there, and he had this very fast striding left hand, and people would be all around...he would be going through one of these hours. And as I said, if someone gave him five dollars, that meant that a lot of other people kicked in, and he'd wind up with a pocket-full of a money.

But he'd be sitting there playing, and if it was quiet in there, the minute you walked in the door (this room was way in the back), you could hear it. And I'd go straight back in there. I would walk in, and Toby would be taking a drink with his right hand and striding with his left, and sitting
Malachi - 68

sideways, and he'd look up at me and say, 'Hi, John, how you doin'?' -- his left hand is going a mile a minute. 'Did you work tonight? Did you see so-and-so-and-so today?' or something. And I'd exchange some quick hello's with him. And he'd have his drink, and he'd probably sit there playing a couple of choruses with just his left hand. Then he'd go back into it, then finally finish that hour. I don't know who was keeping time for him, but afterwards everybody would be shaking their head in amazement.

One of the people who used to come up that I remember is a guy named Marty Emerson, who was a trombone player, him and a guy named Jack Schaeffer, who was a trumpet player. I think Jack Schaeffer went to Las Vegas. I don't know if he's still around or not. But Marty Emerson is now Secretary of the international body of the American Federation of Musicians. If you ever get the International newspaper or have anything to do with the American Federation of Musicians, Marty Emerson is the Secretary, and he's a big wheel there now.

Anyway, those were just some memorable days in shaping, you know, every approach that I had to music. And these associations... You aren't aware of it when they're happening, but they have an indelible stamp on you for life. The big bands and the little band that I had...
Incidentally, Frank Wess, the tenor saxophone player and
Malachi - 69

flautist, as I said before, he worked with this little band we had when he was 14. By the time he was 15 years old, 15 or 16, he was called to work in one of these bands -- Bill Baldwin's band, that used to work at the Colonnade there. And being as young as he was, he was a phenomenon, too, because he became the spark of the band, you know, being a tenor saxophone player. And I guess, in a way, he can be thankful to Billy Roberts for turning him on to playing the tenor saxophone.

So many things happened. In the meantime, Osie Johnson, who later became a fabulous musician, much under-rated... I won't say he was under-rated, but he was never credited. Well, one reason, I guess he didn't live long enough; he passed away at a relatively early age. But he was one of the first drummers that I knew that was a real drummer. Excuse me... Before that, fellows used to have an expression. If you had 15 men in the band, you had 14 musicians and a drummer. Because the drummer was always supposed to be a dummy that didn't know how to do anything but beat time. But Osie Johnson was different, because he could write. And in this little band that we had, right along with me he was writing arrangements of all kinds. He used to love Earl Hines' band, and he would copy a lot of Earl Hines' things off the records.
But you gave him some help. Right?
Malachi - 70
Well...
That's what he said.

Yeah, he says that. When you associate with somebody like that, you... I guess you are helping them in a way. Yeah, I don't remember things that he said. But he and I worked together, and by me being the pianist, perhaps he would talk to me about some chord or some voicing. You know, when you're young like that, unless you've got some kind of ego to say, "Well, I helped do this..." I have a lot of musicians that I know give me a lot of credit for having done this and that, and a lot of times I don't even remember. But I have had musicians makes statements that if it were not for me, they would never have been this or that. But as far as I'm concerned, I always look on musicians, when I'm working with them, as fellow musicians. And whether I know more or whether they're learning from me or something, I never give a thought to. If we're playing together, we're playing together! And I had a lot of respect for Osie, you know.

I think a person learns from every musician that he works with. Just because he was playing a couple of years longer, or ten years or whatever, it doesn't mean that you can't learn something from another musician. See, I teach now, and I've taught my students "You think that you're studying from me. I'm studying from you at the same time!"
Malachi - 71
So anyone, Osie and I were very good friends. His mother is Charlotte Fillmore, who is the darling of a lot of musicians in New York right now. Clark Terry...
His daughter?
No, I said Clark Terry... His mother.
Oh, Osie's mother.

Osie's mother, who is very much around right now. Whenever Clark Terry or Zoot Sims or a lot of other musicians come to Washington, they go straight to Charlotte Fillmore's house. Or else they call her home, she has them over for dinner and all that. If you ever talk to any of them, if you ask about Charlotte Fillmore, which is Osie Johnson's mother... I am going to call her soon and talk to her. When I do, she'll probably give it to me for not having talked to her since Christmas, because Osie's daughter was here Christmas, and she's sort of a godchild of mine, and I was over... She lives in California now, and she comes home to visit her grandmother. I pick her up at the airport and I go over to see Charlotte. And she always says, 'Where have you been? You've been treating me terrible. You don't come by.' Then she'll go on and tell me all about what's happening in the music world, because she knows what's happening from California to New York, just like I do. Charlotte, Osie's mother, is...I'm sure she's approaching 80. She's somewhere
Malachi - 72
close to her eightieth birthday, and she gets around as much as anybody in this town! She does a lot of civic work, you know. She's gotten awards from the White House and everything.

Anyway, Osie was one of those people who was just an excellent musician. He worked with Earl Hines' band... Well, after our band, we had this... I don't want to get ahead of myself here. After the guys began to go into the Army, Osie Johnson, Leonard Phillips and a fellow named Harry Curtis, an alto player (Leonard Phillips, the trumpet player, Osie Johnson, the drummer), Tommy Potter (bass), and a young tenor saxophone player who was 18 then, and he was also at Armstrong High School, and his name was Charlie Rouse -- we formed a band, a six-piece band. We worked at this famous club, as far as Washington goes, called the Crystal Caverns. It's the one I was telling you about where Jimmy Mundy wrote this tune called "Cavernism." Well, we worked there, and this was in 1942. It was during the war...

We had a very good little band, and Osie and I wrote some six-piece arrangements that all the musicians that came from around the country, and came to the Howard Theatre, and they would come down and hear us, and admire us for sounding like a big band. But at this time, Osie and I were experimenting with all kinds of arrangements. Sometimes on ballads behind
Malachi - 73

singers or something, we would write things with the tenor saxophone, the alto and the trumpet, and maybe have a bass (?) or a fourth part to be like a horn, and we'd stretch the harmonies out. It was a very nice little band. And people came down there...

Even John Hammond came down, who was then responsible for the Basie band, I understand... The thing that John Hammond didn't like about our band was that we didn't play enough Blues, you know. And at that particular time, we were experimenting with all kinds of chords and harmonies, and we weren't that much into the Blues as we should have been. We didn't realize just what Blues really meant. We played some Blues and stuff like that, but we were more or less into experimenting and arranging things more intricate with rhythms, and we were listening to people like Jimmy Lunceford and Duke Ellington, Earl Hines. We actually played more Blues-type things when we had the big band, because we played more Basie-type things. But in this little band, we were experimenting with all kinds of voicings and stuff.

Anyway, we had this band... After about... Almost I guess in the second year, about eighteen months, Trummy Young, who had been the trombone player with Jimmy Lunceford's band, decided to get a band of his own. He had been inspired by Louis Jordan, who had gotten a little band -- he called it the
Malachi - 74

Tympany Five. And Louis Jordan was hot as the proverbial firecracker, and he was making a whole lot of money. And there were a lot of musicians that were with Jimmy Lunceford who were disenchanted with what he was doing. Because Jimmy Lunceford, from what I understand, was sort of like a schoolmaster. He had this good band, a very disciplined band, and good musicians. But as far as him giving them any money that they rightfully deserved, he didn't seem to be so willing to do that. So he began to lose people like Trummy Young or Willie Smith, all the guys...

Anyway, Trummy, after having met me in Tommy Miles' band that he had been a former member of... Because whenever that band came in town, they'd come around and see Tommy Miles, and I got to know him. When he left Jimmy Lunceford, he came down to see me, and he knew that I was doing some writing and everything. He told me about this idea that he had about getting this little band together. He spoke about a voicing. where he was going to use trombone, tenor and alto. After hearing our little band down there, he felt that I could really get a good sound with that. Trummy always could play unusually high on the trombone...
I was really a little reluctant at first, because I was never one to be over-confident about what I could do. So he just told me, said, 'Man, you can do it. Come on, you won't
Malachi - 75
regret it." Anyway, he finally talked me into it.

In the meantime, a month or so before that, Osie Johnson had been called into the Navy. So that kind of put a dent in our band -- although we got a very good drummer, a guy named Charlie Buck. But it wasn't the same thing. The idea had kind of fallen. So I decided that I would take this thing on.

In the meantime, he said that he would like to have Tommy Potter as the bass player, and this fellow Harry Curtis, the alto saxophone player, who had been the first alto saxophone player in the Tommy Miles band. So the the three of us left the club. The club-owner was very disappointed with us, because it was during the War, and musicians weren't that easy to get! And we had a good band. Anyway, Trummy put a stop to all of that.
What happened was, I turned the band over to Leonard Phillips, and it later became Phil Phillips' band. I gave him all the arrangements that I had everything.

So we got this little band together... While I was still here, I started writing these arrangements for Trummy, and he stayed down here and we duplicated some or most of those arrangements. We did "Margie" and "Down By The Old Mill Stream" -- some of the popular Jimmy Lunceford things. When we felt like the band was ready, we were rehearsed and everything, Trummy set this gig up and said we were going...
Malachi - 76
[PAUSE]

One day Trummy walked in the rehearsal, and he told us about this gig that he had. As a matter of fact, the agent had been waiting for the band to rehearse and be ready before he booked us. So I guess Trummy must have called him and told him we was ready to move. And Trummy came to the rehearsal one day and said, "We're going to Chicago. But on the way to Chicago, we've got two weeks in Kalamazoo, Michigan, we'll play that, and then we'll go to Chicago." So never having... The furthest that I had been away from Washington at that particular time was New York, which was a short time when I think Osie, Tommy Potter, I think Charlie Rouse might have been with us when we went up just for a holiday sometime during the time we were working at the Caverns, I guess. But other than that, as far as places like Chicago and California, at that time they were places that were far, far away.

So that the idea of going to Chicago, much as I had heard about it... And that was from listening to Earl Hines at the Grand Terrace, listening to Roy Eldridge at...oh, I forgot the name of the place Roy Eldridge used to play in Chicago, but I think it was on Wabash Avenue. I used to get him sometimes at 3 or 4 o'clock in the morning from out there. The tune that I remember him playing most times was a thing called "Heckler's Hop." But that was about the extent of my knowing what
Malachi - 77
Chicago was all about, other than knowing about Al Capone and people like that. I knew it was the gangster capital of the world! Yeah, we were pretty excited about it.

So we boarded the train here one morning, headed for Kalamazoo, Michigan. We got there, and it was a nice place for us to break the band prior to going to Chicago, because a couple of weeks there, and the band got a chance to actually be exposed, and the audience was very... You know, everybody seemed to know Trummy Young at that particular time.

We left there and we went to Chicago to play a place called the Capital Lounge down on State Street. That was like just a paradise for a musician to be in, because at that particular time it seemed like everybody was in Chicago... There were names all over the place. We were at the Capital Lounge along with Muggsy Spanier's group, and the first time I'd ever... I'd heard about Muggsy Spanier, but I'd never met him. He was a very fine old man. He used to talk to us a lot, and he loved to come down in the dressing room with his horn and play little things, and say 'How do you like this?' - - and he'd play some pretty little things. And he played beautiful horn, you know. He had this little group that played opposite us.
Then round the corner, Roy Eldridge had a band at a place called the Preview. He had his brother, Joe, and a drummer
Malachi - 78

whose name I can't remember... Everybody used to call him Dr. Fu(?). I can't remember his name. But he and, as I said, Joe Eldridge. There was a fellow named Roswell Gayle(?), who is in California now, who is a pianist, and he's turned actor -- as a matter of fact, he's had some acting parts in pictures now, I understand; a very good friend. There was a guy who was playing bass, and he was a former saxophone player. I can't remember his name either. He smoked a cigar a lot. But anyway, they were there with Roy Eldridge. And the Preview had a revolving stage where the guys played and the stage went around, and I had never seen that happen before.

I don't know... Each one of those places had at least two bands. The Preview was on Randolph Street, and we were on State Street. Right down the street from Roy Eldridge, on the right, was a guy who later became a very famous accordion player, whose name was Art Van Damme. He had one of the most popular ever accordion trios, and he used to be fantastic on the accordion. Down the street from him was the band that recorded Dizzy's...
Boyd Raeburn?

Boyd Raeburn. Boyd Raeburn had a big band right down on the corner. In that same place, Pete Brown, a very popular alto saxophone player back then, and played... He was one of the big names on the alto saxophone during that time. He had
Malachi - 79

a group. Down the street in the Sherman Hotel was Cab Calloway's band. Duke Ellington was playing the Stephens Hotel. There was just music everywhere, with all kinds of names. And between shows, we'd just go around and meet all these people. And I got to know so many musicians who became lifetime friends, who ended up being friends.

Then, the fact is that Chicago at that particular time, like all other cities, had its sections where the Blacks lived and congregated. Now, this was all downtown in what they call the Loop in Chicago. But afterwards, everybody went out to the South Side, White and Black, and that's when they had clubs out there like the... They had a club called the Rhumboogie where Coleman Hawkins was playing. There was a club where Joe Williams used to work, one of the most popular... I can't remember now. I'll think of it after a while. [ED: CLUB DE LISA] There was a theatre, the Regal Theatre, where there was always somebody playing. And they had so many little places on the South Side where musicians were playing. In the hotels where we lived there were musicians playing.

This is actually where I really met my very good and lifetime friend, Al Hibbler, the singer. Since then we've had many associations. I really met him out there, and he and I became very fast friends. It was just an enjoyable time.
Malachi - 80

We went into the Capital Lounge in December, and we stayed there up through about March, I believe. And we left there and went to New York, 52nd Street, and opened up in another...if not more so. Because 52nd Street... The block we were working on, there were at least seven or eight clubs right on that block, and they were all right next door to each other. And each club had at least two or three bands working there.

On 52nd Street, we opened at a place called the Yacht Club. In the Yacht Club, our band worked opposite Dizzy Gillespie. Dizzy Gillespie and Coleman Hawkins had a band, and Jackie Miles playing drums, Oscar Pettiford on bass, and Clyde Hart on piano. There was a woman, Una Mae Carlisle, who sang in there. They had three attractions.

Across the street was Billie Holiday. I think Max Roach had a group over there, or Max Roach was playing with somebody over there or something. I don't remember who the other group was. But next door was Art Tatum, Red Allen, somebody else... These groups changed around quite a lot. A lot of times I'm thinking... I remember working in the club... Later on, after Roy came back from Chicago, he worked there, and Red Allen went across the street. It was one of those kind of things, you know. It was three groups in the Three Deuces.
After Dizzy and Coleman Hawkins left the Yacht Club, I
Malachi - 81
think Coleman Hawkins went into the Three Deuces, and Hot Lips Page came into the Yacht Club. The bands were always switching around like that.

I remember one time Coleman Hawkins had a band in a place called Kelly's Stables. Once they recorded this thing with Dizzy Gillespie, and I remember Leo Parker was playing alto saxophone on that. "Disorder At The Border" -- there were four sides they did, I think.

There was just music everywhere. Moreso, there were musicians that you could actually, between sets, go around to a bar they had called the White Roses where everybody congregated, and guys would go around there and just drink. And you know, standing next to Art Tatum or whomever, or shaking hands with this one and saying "Hello" to this one... For a young musician, you really felt like you were into something.

We stayed down there until about June, I believe. Then we went in and we did a week in the Apollo Theatre. I think right after that was when I got a message from home with some greetings that Uncle Sam had called me to go into the Armed Services. Which broke my heart! Because I was the last person in the world who felt like I wanted to go in the Armed Services and leave 52nd Street. Not only that, but for other reasons, I felt like I had no business in anybody's Army
Malachi - 82

fighting Germans or Japanese or anybody else who I'd never had no association with. Or, in fact, as a young man that I was then, thinking that way, I felt like if I was going in the Army, I should have been going down to Mississippi somewhere to fight somebody down there. At the same time, I knew that after the War was over, these same people that we were going over there to fight would come over here, and they would be doing everything from calling me a nigger to getting a better job than me or anything else. You know? So I just felt like I had no place in nobody's Army. Because to me, going in the Army meant that you were making a commitment to lay down you life for something, and that just didn't make sense to me. With my optimism about being a musician and looking forward to everything at that particular time, the height of what... I really saw that things were really opening up to where I had really begun to feel like a musician. Before then, it had been something I was doing. But it hadn't been too long that I had committed myself to being a professional musician.

Anyway, I went home and went for induction, passed it with flying colors, and they put me in the Navy and sent me to Great Lakes. I went up to Great Lakes, and this where Osie Johnson and Willie Smith, Clark Terry, the brothers... The first alto saxophone player with Basie and his brother.
Earle Warren, you mean?
Malachi - 83
No.
Tab Smith?
No.
You mean the Royals? Marshall Royal...
Marshall Royal and Ernie Royal. All of these people were up there in the band, you know. They had this band which was a dynamite little band.
Was that Willie Smith's band?

I don't know whose it was. I guess it was some person that was an Army officer or something. It wasn't any of their band. They were just... But anyway, when I went up there they had this band. And immediately, they started to talk to me about coming over, and there was the opportunity for coming over and joining that band with all these people in it. I'd just left 52nd Street, and I was out here with no...you know, without that kind of discipline and all that.

Plus, the first night that we went in the Navy, after we went through some kind of cleaning inspection -- that's what you go through when you first enter there... Then that night, we were in these barracks, and the barracks were all Black guys in there. And an incident happened that just made me almost convinced that something had to happen for me to get out of there. We had a bunch of new recruits, all of us. There must have been at least 50-100 of us in this particular
Malachi - 84
barracks. So, just having come off the street and everything, everybody's talking about what's happening, and guys kidding each other about what their old lady was doing back...
[END OF TAPE 2, SIDE 2]
The guys were kidding each other, telling each other what their old lady's doing back home. And the guy who was left in the street, everybody referred to him as Jody, you know...!
Jody?
Yeah. What it really meant was, they had an expression called "Joe, the Grinder." "Joe the Grinder's got your old lady!" But the short for that was Jody -- "Jody got your old lady." Just kiddin'!

So finally, this little guy comes in. He looks like he's probably 5'5", I guess. Small-built fellow, slight fellow. He's got on a uniform, and I don't know exactly what his position was, but he was an officer of some kind. He came in and said, "All right, you fellows. I want to welcome you to the Navy, so-and-so and so-and-so." Then he went on to break it down to what you were doing, and he said, "These lights go out at 8 o'clock, and you're supposed to go to sleep. There's going to be no activity in here afterwards," etcetera. Everybody's quiet and listening. You know this is really your
Malachi - 85
feeling of being in the Service, and he's running this speech down.

Anyway, he split, and I guess it must have been about a half-hour or 45 minutes before bedtime. So the guys... This really meant that you start getting undressed and everything. So anyway, sure enough, at 8 o'clock the lights went out, and the guys are laying up there in these bunks. So somebody makes a crack about something, everybody else laughs, and somebody else says something. Finally, the guys are buzzin' and they're talking and talking and talking. So somebody would say something else funny... And you know, the guys are talking!

So all of a sudden, the lights came on bright, and this, this little guy is standing up there with his legs spread apart and his hands on his hips. And he pointed his finger and said, "All right, you colored boys, you all knock that shit off in here. If I have to come back in here again, I'm going to run you all around the drill field in your shorts." Now, it's June in Great Lakes. June in Great Lakes is like February or March! You know, it's cold up there. It doesn't start to get warm up there until July or something. So boy, everybody's saying... This guy is saying "You colored boys" -- that really put a thing on us. "What is this?" So I'm laying up there, and I really prayed that night. I said, "Look, I've
Malachi - 86
got to come out of this thing some kind of way. I'm coming out dead or alive!"

Anyway, the next day... For that week... You're in boot camp for a week. They take you through all kinds of inspections. They inspect you for everything from crabs to venereal disease, to all...you know, they go in... One guy looks in... Two doctors, one looks in one ear and the other one looks in the other one, and if they don't see each other, they say "Okay"!

Anyway, about the middle of the week, we go to these doctors in this building. I didn't know what that was all about. But I went in there, and there was a big table with these guys sitting up there with the braid(?) and everything, and they started asking me questions about how I felt about the Navy and the Armed Service, and this and that. So I just gave them some straight answers about how I felt about everything. And they looked at my thing and said, "You're a musician." "Yeah." "Where you working?" I told him.

About that time, I think somewhere around in there... Eddie Heywood is somebody who'd just gotten busted. I think he'd gotten busted in California somewhere. But it was somebody who had just got busted in California for some drugs or something. Pot. So one of them left over to the other one, and sort of whispered something in his ear. And this guy
Malachi - 87

looked at me and said, "Do you do any drugs?" And a lightbulb came on in my head, and I said, "Yes, sir!" He said, "You want to tell us all about it?" I said, "Look, I have a wife and two kids at home, and my mother and father, and they're Christian people, and I don't want them to know nothing about what I've been into in New York." They said talked to each other, and they turned around to me and said, "Look, John, we'll guarantee you that whatever you say to us will remain here in this room, and that the Navy does not want to hurt you in any way," and so on and so on and so on. And when they said that, my heart leaped for joy, and I let them have it with both barrels.

What it was, I didn't tell them anything. They would ask me things. They asked me did I know anything about heroin and did I know anything about this. And a lot of times... They didn't ask me if I used it -- which I was going to tell them I did anyway. And what I told them, like I knew it in a knowledgeable way. And when I'd do that, they'd nod to each other.

Finally, after a question-and-answer period of about 35 minutes, they told me to go back to my barracks, and they would contact me later. I went back to the barracks, and in a couple of days I was summoned to go back to this (?) place. They said, "Well, John, we've made a decision. We feel that
Malachi - 88

you would do a better service to your country as a civilian than you would as a sailor." So I didn't say anything. They said something like, "What do you think about that?" I said, "Whatever you say, sir" or something like that. I didn't want to express what I was feeling! All I wanted to do was get the hell out of that door, boy. Anyway, they said, "We'll say that everything is taken care of."

Anyway, I went back and... The day that I went in there was a Friday, and the next Saturday they gave me my ticket home and told me to go straight home, that I was under the Navy's care until I got to my door. And my stint in the Navy was eight days.

So I came back home, and I like to scared my wife to death because she had no idea she was going to see me that soon! I just told her, "Well, it must have been your prayers," because actually it was just a series of circumstances that... It was just almost like telling somebody what they wanted to hear. They asked the questions and I answered them, and obviously it was the right time and everything. Because I know so many other guys who tried things to get out, and nothing worked!
Anyway, I came on out. After I was home about a week, a couple of weeks... I don't even know how the news got to New York, but I got this telegram that I still have now, that said
Malachi - 89

"Forming a band. Would like to have you and Tommy Potter come to New York and join the band." I have it here. Sometime I'll show it to you. But it said, "Regards, Billy Eckstine." Right away, I sent him one back, and said "I'm on my way." So this began another phase that we'll go into and talk about later!
John Malachi (Part 2) - (5/6/83):
It's now the sixth of May. I think we left off with that telegram asking you to join the Eckstine band.

Yeah. Which started out to be actually what I always think of as the most important era of my particular musical career. Nevertheless, before I get into that, I would like to go back and talk about some other things. Because when you are talking about your career or your life or something like that, it's impossible, I think, to just go in a straight chronological line and bring out everything that happened. Because while one thing is happening, something else is happening at the same time. So right now, I'd like to make a little digression and talk about some of the piano influences that I probably didn't mention.

I think it was around 1936... My playing had been strongly influenced by Fats Waller and Earl Hines, and somewhere between there I was trying to find a good way to play the piano. As far as a style was concerned, I hadn't thought so much about that; I was always more or less copying everything I heard.

One night, I happened to go to a party. I think it was one of these house rent parties. And it was one of a different kind, that didn't have a piano in there. Strangely enough, I don't know this happened, but this place had a jukebox. It was in someone's upstairs apartment, and I never
Malachi (2) - 2

will forget it. It was at Sixth and M Streets Northwest in Washington. I was at this party, and I think that probably that was some point of maturity as far as music was concerned and a turning point, because... They had this record on there, and someone put a nickel in the jukebox. I heard this piano playing, and I heard this lady singing. Then it turned out to be Teddy Wilson playing the piano and Billie Holiday singing. I learned later that the trumpet player was Roy Eldridge and the tenor saxophone player was Chu Berry.

But back to this piano. So I listened, and I hadn't heard anyone play with that kind of a sound. To me it was just different and it was actually a very pretty sound that I hadn't heard that style... I just kind of went ape over it. They had a flip side to it; I think the flip side was a thing called "Eenie-Meenie-Minee-Moe" -- "Eenie-Meenie-Minee-Moe/Catch Trouble by the Toe" or something like that. But anyway, Billie Holiday with the same people backing her up.

So I left that party that night, jubilated(sic) by what I had heard. And two or three days later, I was over at the tenor saxophone player's house that I grew up with, who later played in the little band that we got together. He and I had grown up together, and we'd been friends since I guess we were 11 or 12 years old. I was over at his house, and I was telling him about this pianist that I heard. We were
Malachi (2) - 3

discussing it. And he knew about Chu Berry... He asked me who the saxophone player was. I said, "I don't know who the saxophone player was," but the piano player's name was on the jukebox and it was Teddy Wilson. He said, "Teddy Wilson? I don't think I've heard of him."

Anyway, while we were sitting there talking... Oh, I told him, I said, "This guy plays pretty piano, but it's kind of in a slow vein..." I didn't know to use the term (?) or whatever. But I said I didn't think he could play very fast, like a lot of things that Earl Hines does.

So while we were talking about this, on the radio in one of the afternoon programs (I wouldn't have no idea whose program it was) came this record of an old tune called "China Boy." And it turned out to be the Benny Goodman Trio. And the guy said later it was Teddy Wilson, Benny Goodman and Gene Krupa. And that really blew my mind. So for I guess the next... That was 1936. Probably for the next eight years, my whole thing was wrapped up in Teddy Wilson, with maybe little sprinkles of a run or something from Art Tatum that I could find or that someone would show me. Billy Taylor and I used to sit and listen to Art Tatum a lot, and we'd try to catch runs and things. But basically, the style that I was trying to play was Teddy Wilson. And he also had a way of playing his left hand which involved tenths in his left hand that I
Malachi (2) - 4
hadn't heard anyone do like the way he did before.

In the interim of this, there were some pianists around town that I liked very much. There was one guy, a fellow from New York who had come down here and he made Washington his home for a number of years. His name was Harold Francis. Later he worked with the Ink Spots for a while. I think he died in the Fifties. Anyway, Harold was probably the most literate of the Black pianists around town, because at that particular time there were a lot of good piano players around, but none of them could read very well.

Harold used to play a lot of shows at the Howard Theatre, and at times he would substitute for Earl Hines or some of the other pianists at the Howard Theatre that came to the dances. Because it was kind of proper for the leaders, if they were pianists, to play a few numbers and have a substitute pianist. They would go off the bandstand -- where they would go, I don't know. Then they would come out and maybe play another specialty. Harold showed me a lot about how Teddy Wilson was playing, because he played that style himself.
There was also another fellow around that I used to listen to a lot, although he played more like Earl Hines. He's still around, a fellow named Dick Hopkins. I listened to him a lot.
Then there was another guy. His name was Clyde Wright.
Malachi (2) - 5

He was from Roanoke, Virginia. He was on the pudgy side; everybody called him "Fats" -- Fats Wright. But he was an excellent piano player in every respect. We were talking one day, and I was talking about Teddy Wilson and Art Tatum, and I was saying how these guys played these tenths. I said, "Boy, I sure wish I could play tenths." And Fats also played tenths himself. That's how the subject came up. Because I was listening to him play, and I was admiring them tenths.

Fats was the kind of a guy, if you didn't know him well, you'd think he was always mad at you. When I said something about the tenths, he said something to the effect, "What the hell is wrong with you? Why can't you play tenths?" I said, "My hand is not that large." He said, "Hell, your hand is bigger than mine!" I couldn't believe that, and he took his hand and put it up against mine, and actually my fingers were I guess a sixteenth of an inch longer than his. So right away, I said, "Well, how the hell do you do it?" He said, "Try to play them and stretch your hand" -- then he showed me how to do some exercises and things. And I started to play these tenths.

It was guys like that, that really, when I think of musicians... People ask me "Who taught you how to play?" or "Where did you learn to play?" or something. And I said, "Well, I learned from everybody that I've ever known. Every
Malachi (2) - 6

musician that I've ever played with, whether I was better than he wasn't or whether I wasn't, I learned something from him." And I think that's the way all musicians are -- if they would admit it to themselves, you know.

But this was, I guess, around in the late Thirties. Then around 1941 (I think it was '41, or it might have been '40, somewhere between '41 and '40), I had the extreme pleasure -- it was like a dream come true -- to meet Art Tatum. It so happens that a fellow that I mentioned before that had a band, Booker Coleman, had been friends with Art Tatum for years. He had known him since he was a very young man, so much to the extent that Art always called Booker's mother...he called her "Mama" too. And there were so many incidents where I would be at Mrs. Coleman's house... Art used to stay there a lot when he came to Washington. And Booker and Art would get to arguing about anything. After a while, another guy would come in, and I would be introduced to him, and they would have the same kind of conversation, and I would find out that he was the defense lawyer. So I always had this impression, I guess from the movies and television, that these guys were archenemies and that they didn't hardly speak to each other otherwise. But I found out that they were great friends and family friends, etcetera.

Anyway, I got this letter from the Navy that these two girls were asking me if I would write to them and state to them what had happened in this case, and these two little girls, it seemed as if their backs had been broken or something. Of course, their parents were dead, and the third party in the car happened to be an uncle who was German, and they had been to New York to pick him up and bring him... This was his first time in the United States.
Anyway, this trial... I was up there two or three times - three times, I believe. The last time I was there, they had
Malachi (3) - 51

me on the witness stand, and the defense lawyer asked me what condition was the highway in. Well, the Pennsylvania Turnpike I remember is about 300-some miles long. So I made mention of the fact, I said, "The turnpike is 300 miles long. What do you mean?" He said, "Well, any part of it." He said, "Well, I did see some people doing repair work." And he said "Oh, thank you." And I said, "But..." He said, "That's enough" -- and I stepped down. Another time he asked me some other question as to did I see men working on the highway or did I see anything wrong with the highway. When I would go to explain that this was not happening where the accident happened, I was never allowed to answer that. I would be told by the judge, "You can step down" or he would say, "Well, that's enough."

Well, when I left there, the jury was debating, and the last time I was there... I was playing a gig in Cleveland. It was one of those times when I had gone back to play a job with Al. And I had just gone up to this little town for the trial, and I had to get right back to Cleveland. So the jury was out, and the district attorney told me "Well, we won't need you any more." I said, "Well, okay. But do me a favor and send me a letter or something and let me know how the trial comes out." He said, "Oh, sure I will." I haven't heard from him since. And the last time I saw, the trial was going this
Malachi (3) - 52

kid's way who had caused the accident. He was a Pennsylvania boy, you know. Well, I just surmised that those people are dead, those grown-ups and the kids, nothing you could do about them, and they just... These people lived somewhere out in the Midwest. So I imagine this boy, with the proper amount of money, just walked away clean from the whole thing.

But that was quite an experience, and it ended my days with Dakota Staton. It wasn't long after that, that I got a call from Gloria Lynne. I had an engagement with her in California. This turned out to be a rather strange kind of engagement, because I don't know what happened out there, but Gloria's behavior was very erratic. The club started off with people just loving her to death, the business was good, the place was packed and everything. But I never did understand quite what happened out there. After about the second night, she started...she would go on stage and do two or three numbers, then just walk off and not do anything else. So finally, it wound up with the manager having to call Wilt Chamberlain, the basketball, who owned the club -- the club was called Basin Street West. At that particular time, I think he was also the owner of Small's Paradise in New York. He had to call him, and there was quite a bit of controversy.
In the interim of all this, in my attempt to find out what was happening and talk to her, she seemed intimidated by
Malachi (3) - 53

me... She and I had an argument, and she told me I was fired. So I made mention of the fact that I was in California, and what was I going to do about going back home. So she promptly told me that she didn't care what I did about getting back home!

So I went to the Musicians Union, and I have to say that's one of the few times that the union has really proved to be on my side of the fence. I went to the Musicians Union, and I can't say enough for the local in Los Angeles -- I think it's Local 47. I went and expressed my case to them, and they told me, "Don't worry about a thing. You go back to your hotel, and go to work tonight, just like you were going, and if she doesn't want you to play, you stay there for an hour, and then go back to your hotel or wherever you want to go." So I did this for a couple of nights, and each day I would approach her. What happened, after about three days, he said, "You don't even need to go over there any more. Just stay around until the end of the engagement, and you will get your money and your plane fare back home."

So this I did, and while I was there, I have to say it proved out to be a very nice three-week vacation in California at Gloria Lynne's expense, and I had my plane fare back. I had a good time, because there were a lot of musicians that I knew out there that I hung out with. One of the guys that I
Malachi (3) - 54

did a lot of hanging out with was a fellow named Kenny, who at that particular time was Nancy Wilson's husband. We went and saw the Muhammad Ali fight -- I think it was one of the major fights of his career -- with Sonny Liston. There were just so many things that happened...

Anyway, after that, I flew back to Washington, and I started working in a club that was owned by a fellow named Pete Lambros, but the main attraction there was a guitarist whose name was Charlie Byrd. I worked up there for I guess the better part of two years. But while I was there, I did some other miscellaneous engagements with people, one of them being Joe Williams. I did a thing, I was back in California again with him. We were there for something like two or three weeks.

After that we did a club in Chicago, called I think Basin Street. I had a trio there, I believe... Yeah, I sent to Washington and I got a bass player Fred Williams, and a drummer, Harold Chavis. I think we had a couple of weeks there in Chicago which proved to be pretty nice.

After that... I guess this is about up to 1965. Since then, everything has been pretty much around Washington, D.C. There have been groups and there have been trios, and a lot of things that I've done here with the better musicians around Washington.
Malachi (3) - 55

I had a beautiful experience in a club that Bill Harris, the guitarist that was with the group called The Clovers for quite a long time, as a matter of fact, the extent of their career... Bill Harris opened a club here, and he called it the Pig Foot. I was asked to come in and be musical director for the club, or officiate the entertainment. We started a workshop there. I met a lot of fine, young, up-and-coming, talented musicians. Some of them are really well on their way to making their mark. Others are still doing very well, and are making their way. And those kind of things make you feel good.

I can think of names like George Johnson, who turned out to be Eddie Jefferson's protege, and who never ceases to give me credit for having been responsible for that... Eddie Jefferson, the singer, who had such an untimely death... The singer that was with James Moody of "Moody's Mood For Love" fame, who was a very good friend of mine. And George Johnson seems to think that I had a lot to do with their relationship. Which he and Eddie became very good friends, and a a result of it, he met James Moody, and now he has the job with James Moody that Eddie Jefferson had with James Moody.
There are other people. There's a singer, Rod Willoughby, who is well on the way to becoming a very popular singer, and I am looking for big things from him.
Malachi (3) - 56

I met a young musician during these workshops that I came to know, and he always seemed to have a more than usual enthusiasm about the history of Jazz, and I must say he was more knowledgeable... Few people I know are more knowledgeable about what has happened, especially young people, in Jazz history than this young man. If he's not talking about some incident that happened, he's always asking a question about it. And at times there are things he knows and says that are enlightening to me, or would be to anybody who is three times his age. And this young man's name is Bryant DuPre, and he happens to be responsible for everything that I'm saying here, because he's talked to me about it for some time and sort of been a catalyst in getting me to do this particular thing.

I guess, to sum this up, I am sure that there's always something you forget or that doesn't come to mind. As I was talking to him the other day, I was saying that nobody's life goes in a straight line. And there are so many incidents and people that in a situation like this you don't think to mention. I'm sure after this is over, I'm going to say, 'Why didn't I say so-and-so and so-and-so?' But I think I'm going to wind this up right now.
What I'd like to do, if it's agreeable with Bryant, is have a question-and-answer period with him. He's been listening to all of this, and I'm sure there are some things
Malachi (3) - 57

that he knows or has been reminded of that I wasn't thinking about saying, and we will probably do a lot of backtracking. But all in all, I hope I've said something that's worthwhile to some people who perhaps... Especially young people who wasn't around at certain times when certain musicians who were around. And if I've made them a little more knowledgeable about what was happening in this world of Jazz.
So right now, I think we'll close this down, and we'll have some...
[END OF 5 MAY 1983 SESSION]
This is May 8, 1983, at John's house in Washington, D.C., and you had some other things you wanted to say.

Yeah. In talking about the Eckstine band, I mentioned a lot of individuals. In retrospect, I realize that I didn't say enough about some other important people that I could have said some things about.

I'll talk about the arrangers. The principal arranger in the band was Jerry Valentine. He did most of the arranging. Another arranger was the trombone player, another trombone player. His name was...well, we called him Chippie Alcott. Chippie before that had played around with... I think when he came to us, he came to us from Tiny Bradshaw's band. Anyway,
Malachi (3) - 58
Chippie did some of the writing. And I did, of course.

But the other major writer, who joined us about three months after the band had started in 1944, was a very fine arranger -- his name was Tadd Dameron. Tadd was from Cleveland, Ohio, and an arranger with a very unique style of arranging, and was another one of the indelible stamps on the band. While he was with us, one of the things that he wrote was a composition of Billy Eckstine called "I Want To Talk About You." He was the composer of "Our Delight," another up-tempo instrumental that we had. He also made us an arrangement on the the thing that Benny Goodman did, he called it "Good Enough To Keep"...
"Air Mail Special."

"Air Mail Special." Which was a Charlie Christian tune. We had a very fine arrangement on that. And while he was with us, one of his pieces that later became a standard was a thing called "Good Bait." And any number of other things that Tadd wrote for the band. In listening to his arrangements and everything, they also made a profound impression on my musicianship as a writer and as a pianist.

After our stint in California, where we played at the Plantation out there in Watts... I mentioned the fact that Budd Johnson was with the band. Budd Johnson did some arranging also. When we got back East, Budd left the band in New York and Dexter rejoined us. We had another...

segments.chapter: Childhood and first piano
segments.title: Opening: Bryant DuPre interview at Malachi's Washington home, 5 May 1983
segments.summary: The interviewer announces the date and place and hands over to Malachi.

segments.chapter: Childhood and first piano
segments.title: Born in Red Springs; seeing music through the piano and the hymn book
segments.summary: Malachi describes the grandmother's pump organ, being quieted as a toddler with a hymn book, and his sense that a gift is really a love for something.

segments.chapter: Childhood and first piano
segments.title: The Big House, the log cabin, the move to Durham and his mother's schooling
segments.summary: He recalls the family homes in Red Springs, his siblings, the move to Durham and his mother teaching him to read and count before school.

segments.chapter: Childhood and first piano
segments.title: His mother sings her brothers' Sears-order instrument parts
segments.summary: His mother tells of her eight brothers playing trombone, cornet and bass horn by the fire, and sings out each part so he learns to hear harmony.

segments.chapter: Childhood and first piano
segments.title: Fooling with an aunt's little organ in Durham
segments.summary: Whenever he finds a keyboard he sits down to play, an attraction he cannot explain.

segments.chapter: Childhood and first piano
segments.title: Moving to Washington: Deanwood, two rooms, repeating Fifth Grade at Garrison
segments.summary: His father goes ahead to find work, the family follows to Deanwood then cramped rooms in the city, and Malachi is held back a grade.

segments.chapter: Childhood and first piano
segments.title: Father brings home a five-dollar piano; Uncle Jim's five-dollar offer
segments.summary: Just before he turns thirteen a used piano arrives, and Uncle Jim promises five dollars to the first child to play something; Malachi learns Lift Every Voice and Sing.

segments.chapter: Childhood and first piano
segments.title: Banging the piano every evening and discovering chords
segments.summary: He rushes home daily to the piano and finds that stacking keys gives the harmonies his mother used to sing.

segments.chapter: Childhood and first piano
segments.title: The family gramophone: Bessie Smith, Mamie Smith, Louis Armstrong, Ellington
segments.summary: The household records he picked out on the piano, including Sleepy Time Down South and Ring Dem Bells.

segments.chapter: Childhood and first piano
segments.title: Shore Junior High and a schoolmate who plays Fats Waller stride
segments.summary: A slightly younger pianist at Shore Junior High plays Waller tunes with both hands, and Malachi tries to copy him.

segments.chapter: Childhood and first piano
segments.title: At Terrell Junior High, a four-string guitarist friend and a first small repertoire
segments.summary: He sneaks onto the assembly piano, meets a guitarist, and they work up a few pieces and shouts.

segments.chapter: Childhood and first piano
segments.title: First house hops (rent parties) during the Depression
segments.summary: He describes the rent parties with soul food and bathtub liquor, and earning around fifty cents with the guitarist.

segments.chapter: Childhood and first piano
segments.title: House-hop pianists: Kid Norfolk, Kid Socks, Toya and Piano Slim
segments.summary: The older pianists who sat in at rent parties, especially the powerful Kid Norfolk, and the Four Dots and Three Keys connections.

segments.chapter: Childhood and first piano
segments.title: James Morgan, the child-prodigy pianist with a WRC radio show
segments.summary: A boyfriend of his Aunt Pearl brings James Morgan, whose playing of popular tunes amazes him; Morgan never left Washington.

segments.chapter: Childhood and first piano
segments.title: No thought of music as a livelihood
segments.summary: Asked what he wanted to be, he says he did not know; the piano was only a toy to him.

segments.chapter: Washington in the 1930s: big bands, lessons, first jobs
segments.title: First date at the Howard Theatre: Shep Allen and Fletcher Henderson's band
segments.summary: At fourteen he takes a girl to the Howard Theatre and sees Fletcher Henderson's band presented by Shep Allen.

segments.chapter: Washington in the 1930s: big bands, lessons, first jobs
segments.title: Chick Webb's band, and learning the front man was Bardu Ali
segments.summary: He thinks Bardu Ali is Chick Webb, later learns Webb was the drummer, and finds he cannot yet pick out the band pianist.

segments.chapter: Washington in the 1930s: big bands, lessons, first jobs
segments.title: Duke Ellington and Sophisticated Lady convince him to play piano for life
segments.summary: Ellington's dominating piano, looks and his solo Sophisticated Lady make Malachi realize he wants the piano more than anything.

segments.chapter: Washington in the 1930s: big bands, lessons, first jobs
segments.title: Jack Smith's one and only lesson
segments.summary: His father hires Jack Smith as teacher, then dismisses him on the spot because he arrived drunk and taught without music.

segments.chapter: Washington in the 1930s: big bands, lessons, first jobs
segments.title: Wyn Boyd teaches fundamentals and practical harmony
segments.summary: His new fifteen-cent teacher teaches reading and chords, and Malachi is grateful to his father for the change.

segments.chapter: Washington in the 1930s: big bands, lessons, first jobs
segments.title: Cutting lessons for the movies, then returning to the teacher
segments.summary: He skips lessons for the Howard Theatre, is stopped by his father, asks to go back, and the teacher marvels at what he learned by ear.

segments.chapter: Washington in the 1930s: big bands, lessons, first jobs
segments.title: Substituting for his teacher at a club on E Street
segments.summary: Aged fifteen he fills in for an hour with saxophonist Winbush and drummer Eugene Carroll, his first professional-feeling job.

segments.chapter: Washington in the 1930s: big bands, lessons, first jobs
segments.title: A future brother-in-law who plays fast chromatics, and George McIver
segments.summary: Neighborhood friends, a pianist whose sister studied at Howard and the music-loving George McIver with his kazoo.

segments.chapter: Washington in the 1930s: big bands, lessons, first jobs
segments.title: Hearing Art Tatum records at Stanley's basement
segments.summary: A maintenance man plays Tatum's Emaline and Moonglow, which seems otherworldly to him compared with Fats Waller.

segments.chapter: Washington in the 1930s: big bands, lessons, first jobs
segments.title: The idea of genius and the hunchbacked pianist Toby Walker
segments.summary: He meets the word genius, and describes Toby Walker, a Washington pianist who died at twenty-five.

segments.chapter: Washington in the 1930s: big bands, lessons, first jobs
segments.title: Drummer Leo Gilpoopy hires him for the Atlantic Beer Garden
segments.summary: Just before sixteen he is recruited to play duo seven nights a week at twelve dollars a week.

segments.chapter: Washington in the 1930s: big bands, lessons, first jobs
segments.title: Washington's five big bands: Baldwin, Pete Moss, Hester, Tommy Miles, Booker Coleman
segments.summary: A tour of U Street clubs and bands, including Tommy Miles's Cotton Club band with Trummy Young, Jimmy Mundy and Tyree Glenn.

segments.chapter: Washington in the 1930s: big bands, lessons, first jobs
segments.title: After-hours jam sessions; Frank Higgs makes him play I Got Rhythm in B-flat
segments.summary: Big-band players jam at his beer garden job; a tenor player forces him to play in B-flat, and he learns tunes and chord calls from horn players.

segments.chapter: Washington in the 1930s: big bands, lessons, first jobs
segments.title: Annapolis summer job with trumpeter Roosevelt Williams and Oswald Gibson
segments.summary: Before sixteen he goes to Annapolis for a month's club job and discovers he cannot really read music, especially an act's chordless Butterbeans and Susie parts.

segments.chapter: Washington in the 1930s: big bands, lessons, first jobs
segments.title: Practicing with Oswald Gibson and his first arranging: Song of India
segments.summary: He and the young saxophonist put together a four-piece Tommy Dorsey-style Song of India, which Malachi sees as his first arranging.

segments.chapter: U Street, Jelly Roll Morton, the youth band and the WPA
segments.title: Back in Washington: U Street and the Jungle Inn with Kay Hedgeman
segments.summary: He goes looking for work on U Street and lands at the Jungle Inn run by Miss Lyles, accompanying singer Kay Hedgeman.

segments.chapter: U Street, Jelly Roll Morton, the youth band and the WPA
segments.title: Hired for the band at the Crystal Caverns
segments.summary: The most prestigious U Street nightclub, home of Cavernism, needs a pianist, and he joins an eight-piece show band.

segments.chapter: U Street, Jelly Roll Morton, the youth band and the WPA
segments.title: Fired over Don Redman's Chant of the Weed, then learning the whole show at home
segments.summary: The chordless, advanced score defeats him and the owner lets him go; he buys the show's music and teaches himself, setting a lifelong habit.

segments.chapter: U Street, Jelly Roll Morton, the youth band and the WPA
segments.title: Playing Happy Joe's, a rough Irish bar on Ninth Street
segments.summary: He describes nightly brawls, the shillelagh and playing fast tunes with the doors closed.

segments.chapter: U Street, Jelly Roll Morton, the youth band and the WPA
segments.title: Meeting Jelly Roll Morton, new manager at the Jungle Inn
segments.summary: Miss Lyles introduces him to Jelly Roll Morton, a name that means nothing to him, and Morton plays and name-drops.

segments.chapter: U Street, Jelly Roll Morton, the youth band and the WPA
segments.title: Morton's contempt for Tatum, Ellington and Basie; he hires Malachi to fill in
segments.summary: Malachi hears Morton quarrel with the musicians and dismiss Art Tatum and modern players; because he listens, Morton hires him.

segments.chapter: U Street, Jelly Roll Morton, the youth band and the WPA
segments.title: Playing for Pearl Bailey and Morton's New Orleans show; the Library of Congress sessions
segments.summary: He accompanies the singers, watches Morton's white-audience show with Tiger Rag, and later hears Morton is recording at the Library of Congress.

segments.chapter: U Street, Jelly Roll Morton, the youth band and the WPA
segments.title: Marrying Rhoda at seventeen and leaving high school
segments.summary: Robert Harley's sister Rhoda, whom he first disliked, becomes his wife just after his seventeenth birthday.

segments.chapter: U Street, Jelly Roll Morton, the youth band and the WPA
segments.title: Armstrong High School schoolmates: Oswald Gibson, the Washington brothers and his brother
segments.summary: Younger musicians from Armstrong High's band look up to him as a senior player and gather at his house.

segments.chapter: U Street, Jelly Roll Morton, the youth band and the WPA
segments.title: Billy Roberts forms a youth band; Frank Wess switched to tenor
segments.summary: The guitarist assembles a band of teenagers including Frank Wess and Dude Brown, and tells Wess to play tenor.

segments.chapter: U Street, Jelly Roll Morton, the youth band and the WPA
segments.title: Taking over the band; stock arrangements and Billy White
segments.summary: Roberts loses interest, the kids carry on buying stock arrangements and copying records, and Billy White writes for them.

segments.chapter: U Street, Jelly Roll Morton, the youth band and the WPA
segments.title: Learning to write backgrounds; the war breaks up the youth band
segments.summary: He writes chord backgrounds behind a Hershel Evans solo, develops a system for the brass, and the band ends when Sergeant Price takes members into the Army.

segments.chapter: U Street, Jelly Roll Morton, the youth band and the WPA
segments.title: Joining Tommy Miles's WPA band and writing Opus 403
segments.summary: The WPA arts project recruits Tommy Miles's band; Malachi writes his first big-band piece, named after the 403 dismissal slip.

segments.chapter: U Street, Jelly Roll Morton, the youth band and the WPA
segments.title: WPA band as professional training: daily rehearsal and harmony class
segments.summary: Rehearsing every day with a government-paid harmony teacher became his real training.

segments.chapter: U Street, Jelly Roll Morton, the youth band and the WPA
segments.title: The photograph with Eleanor Roosevelt behind him
segments.summary: At a Bureau of Engraving dance he asks Mrs. Roosevelt to move so a photographer can take his picture, a vanity he later regrets.

segments.chapter: U Street, Jelly Roll Morton, the youth band and the WPA
segments.title: Deciding to be a professional musician; joining the union in 1938
segments.summary: After the Miles band he never again holds another kind of job.

segments.chapter: The Footlight Club and Washington friends
segments.title: The Footlight Club after-hours spot and visiting Ellington and Calloway men
segments.summary: Freddie Woods's after-hours room near the Howard Theatre is where touring stars gather and where older friends Phil and Otto name them.

segments.chapter: The Footlight Club and Washington friends
segments.title: Sammy Woods and Roy Eldridge strolling with a joint; reefer songs
segments.summary: Guitarist Sammy Woods taught him chords, and he recalls Roy Eldridge and Woods playing in the streets while smoking marijuana, plus Cab Calloway's Reefer Man.

segments.chapter: The Footlight Club and Washington friends
segments.title: Paul Jones, Buster McPherson and trumpeter Georgetown Brashears
segments.summary: Local tenor Paul Jones battled visiting saxophonists, and Georgetown held his own against Roy Eldridge but refused to leave Washington.

segments.chapter: The Footlight Club and Washington friends
segments.title: Count Basie's band arrives; meeting Lester Young and the Paul Jones story
segments.summary: Basie's new sound reaches the Howard Theatre and Lester Young, a friend of Phil Phillips, becomes Malachi's acquaintance.

segments.chapter: The Footlight Club and Washington friends
segments.title: All-night playing with Lester Young, who teaches him Wilson-Holiday tunes
segments.summary: After Toby Walker finished, Lester Young would sit with Malachi until morning and teach him the tunes he recorded in New York.

segments.chapter: The Footlight Club and Washington friends
segments.title: Toby Walker playing I Got Rhythm for five dollars
segments.summary: Walker played a fast stride I Got Rhythm for an hour whenever the crowd paid, drinking with one hand and striding with the other.

segments.chapter: The Footlight Club and Washington friends
segments.title: Marty Emerson, Jack Schaeffer and what those associations meant
segments.summary: He names two younger regulars, and says these associations left an indelible mark on his approach to music.

segments.chapter: The Footlight Club and Washington friends
segments.title: Frank Wess goes into Bill Baldwin's band at fifteen
segments.summary: Wess leaves the youth band to become the spark of Baldwin's Colonnade band, for which Malachi credits Billy Roberts's switch to tenor.

segments.chapter: The Footlight Club and Washington friends
segments.title: Osie Johnson, the drummer who wrote arrangements, and learning from every musician
segments.summary: Johnson copied Earl Hines records and wrote for the youth band; Malachi downplays his own help and says he learns from his students too.

segments.chapter: The Footlight Club and Washington friends
segments.title: Osie Johnson's mother, Charlotte Fillmore, hostess to visiting musicians
segments.summary: Charlotte Fillmore is a civic figure in Washington whose house Clark Terry and Zoot Sims visit.

segments.chapter: Trummy Young's band, 52nd Street and the Navy
segments.title: The 1942 six-piece band at the Crystal Caverns; John Hammond wants more blues

segments.chapter: Trummy Young's band, 52nd Street and the Navy

segments.summary: Inspired by Louis Jordan's success and Lunceford's low pay, Trummy Young wants a trombone-tenor-alto sound and talks a reluctant Malachi into joining.

segments.chapter: Trummy Young's band, 52nd Street and the Navy

segments.chapter: Trummy Young's band, 52nd Street and the Navy

segments.summary: Trummy announces the booking, Malachi has never been farther than New York, and the band breaks in for two weeks in Kalamazoo.

segments.chapter: Trummy Young's band, 52nd Street and the Navy
segments.title: The Capital Lounge, Muggsy Spanier, and downtown Chicago's clubs
segments.summary: They play State Street opposite Muggsy Spanier while Roy Eldridge, Art Van Damme, Boyd Raeburn, Cab Calloway and Duke Ellington play nearby.

segments.chapter: Trummy Young's band, 52nd Street and the Navy
segments.title: Chicago's South Side and meeting Al Hibbler
segments.summary: After hours the musicians go to the South Side's Rhumboogie and Regal Theatre, where he befriends singer Al Hibbler.

segments.chapter: Trummy Young's band, 52nd Street and the Navy
segments.title: Opening on 52nd Street at the Yacht Club opposite Dizzy Gillespie and Coleman Hawkins
segments.summary: The band plays the Yacht Club while Hawkins, Gillespie, Billie Holiday, Tatum and Red Allen work neighboring clubs.

segments.chapter: Trummy Young's band, 52nd Street and the Navy

segments.summary: He recalls a Hawkins-Gillespie record with Leo Parker and the bar where musicians mingled between sets.

segments.chapter: Trummy Young's band, 52nd Street and the Navy
segments.title: Draft notice after the Apollo week and his reluctance to serve
segments.summary: Called up just after the band plays the Apollo, he explains why he felt he had no place in anybody's army.

segments.chapter: Trummy Young's band, 52nd Street and the Navy
segments.title: Great Lakes: the Navy band of Willie Smith, Clark Terry and the Royals
segments.summary: At Great Lakes he finds an all-star Navy band that invites him to join but he is unwilling.

segments.chapter: Trummy Young's band, 52nd Street and the Navy

segments.summary: After jokes about Jody, a small officer threatens the Black recruits, and Malachi prays to get out.

segments.chapter: Trummy Young's band, 52nd Street and the Navy

segments.chapter: Trummy Young's band, 52nd Street and the Navy

segments.summary: Eckstine wires asking him and Tommy Potter to join a new band in New York, and Malachi replies he is on his way.
